newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Albright, Malaysia clash on 1948 UN rights accord.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Malaysia clash on 1948 UN rights accord.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright pledged on Monday to fight any attempt to dilute a key international human rights declaration that has come under attack by Malaysia.

The proposal by Prime Minister Mohamed Mahathir to alter the 1948 U.N. universal declaration on human rights was one of two issues on which the United States sparred with Malaysia at a Southeast Asian regional meeting.
The other involved a spirited U.S. denial of Mahathir's charges that U.S. billionaire financier George Soros acted deliberately to destabilise Southeast Asian currency markets.
U.S. officials said it was highly unusual for the chairman and host of a multinational conference -- in this case Malaysia -- to pick public fights with participants.
As a result, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said, Washington felt compelled to defend itself.
Albright, a former ambassador to the United Nations, vowed "the United States will be relentless in its opposition to any attempt to water down that (U.N.) declaration," Burns told reporters.

Speaking to a meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, she argued "it would be a great mistake to believe that these principles of civil liberty, human liberty, freedom and integrity of the individual ... had been the imposed by the West on other regions or cultures of the world," Burns said.
Monday's front-page lead story in Malaysia's New Straits Times said Mahathir may submit a proposal to the United Nations to review the human rights declaration.
He argued that the document, which took effect in December 1948, was the product of the big powers of that era and is no longer suitable.
Mahathir has a reputation as an anti-colonialist and has long resented perceived Western arrogance and imperialism and support for Israel.
Malaysia, an overwhelmingly Moslem country, gained independence from Britain in 1957.
Albright awoke to the newspaper headlines and spent the morning mulling a response, which she delivered at a meeting of the United States and ASEAN's nine member states.
Because of the group's operating procedures, neither Mahathir nor his foreign minister were in the session.
Albright "doesn't think there are religions or cultures or ethical systems that want to tolerate torture or a (negation) of human rights," Burns said.
He said Albright argued that millions of people had died to preserve freedom and the 1948 declaration, crafted following World War Two, "was an expression of hope for a better world".

While the declaration took shape before most ASEAN countries gained independence, the United States "has never accepted this argument that somehow individual rights are not consistent with Asian values," he said.

Also on Monday, Undersecretary of State Stuart Eizenstat delievered the most comprehensive and authoritative U.S. response to a row over Southeast Asia's currency crisis that had been brewing for days.
It was triggered when Mahathir openly accused Soros of leading a speculative assault on southeast Asian currencies, especially those of Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia.
Soros has denied attempts to destabilise Asian currencies.

"Experience suggests that market movements are not dominated by a small number of currency speculators, let alone one person, who happens to be a U.S. citizen," Eizenstat said in remarks to a closed-door session that were later released by the State Department.
"Financial markets detected strains in the economy of one of the ASEAN countries and reacted accordingly."
Burns said Washington felt that "countries need to turn to their own efforts to try to restabilise their currencies."
